endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Conditions must be documented and enforced.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Clear documentation of responsibilities in the context of processes and procedures is necessary to achieve AI solution quality and ethical use.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Create mechanisms to provide protections for whistleblowers who report, based on reasonable belief, when the organization violates relevant laws or poses a specific and empirically well-substantiated negative risk to public safety (or has already caused harm).

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: After deployment, the governance of the AI tool should be specified. In particular, the roles of risk management, periodic auditing, maintenance, and supervision should be assigned

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: Ensuring that all local stakeholders are up to date and competent in the use of AI technology is a shared responsibility between vendors and the leaders of local institutional governance and oversight.

endorsements.title: Health Equity Across the AI Lifecycle (HEAAL) framework
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership; PLOS Digital Health (PMID 38723025, doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000390)
endorsements.quote: This assessment domain entails overseeing potential substantial adverse impacts that may arise after the solution is integrated, identifying stakeholders responsible for managing and controlling the solution throughout its lifecycle, and developing plans for continuous monitoring.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Healthcare organizations should develop comprehensive policies that outline the process(es) and identify the responsible parties for monitoring and evaluating AI tools locally.

endorsements.title: Auditing and Monitoring Artificial Intelligence Systems in Healthcare: A Multilayer Framework for Bias Detection, Explainability, and Regulatory Compliance
endorsements.quote: Healthcare institutions must define who is accountable for bias detection, model updates, incident reporting, and regulatory documentation.

endorsements.title: From Pilot Trap to Institutional Capacity: A Governance Framework for Sustainable Clinical AI Implementation in Health Systems
endorsements.quote: A consistent governance principle nevertheless emerges, whereby sustained clinical deployment requires clearly defined roles, decision rights, and accountability structures linking algorithm development, clinical use, and institutional oversight.

endorsements.title: Governing Patient-Facing AI-Generated Video in Digital Health: A Risk-and-Ethics Matrix for Deployment, Monitoring, and Change Control
endorsements.quote: For institutional use, matrix-guided evaluation should be embedded into release governance such that publication or distribution through official channels requires completed dossier documentation, named sign-off, and versioned approval records.

endorsements.title: Large Language Models in Clinical Trial Recruitment: Sociotechnical and Economic Framework Development Study
endorsements.quote: Clarifying decision rights at each stage can reduce duplication, make accountability visible, and help distinguish whether weak performance reflects model limitations, workflow design failures, or governance bottlenecks.

endorsements.title: From Sensors to Systems: Real-Time Human Performance and Health Monitoring
endorsements.quote: defining clear governance roles (data ownership, access, escalation pathways), embedding monitoring within existing medical and performance workflows rather than alongside them, and agreeing in advance how alerts translate into decisions.

commentary.bottom_line: Twelve sources endorse documenting AI governance roles and decision rights, two frameworks at the must level, but no study has tested whether role mapping changes governance performance or patient outcomes. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and face validity, not on measured effect.

perspectives.view: The endorsing sources are frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries, and none reports data. No study tests the practice, and no study documents how often controls lack a responsible role or what follows. Agreement across 12 sources shows consistent expert opinion, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect.

FUTURE-AI and one auditing commentary ask that roles for risk management, auditing, incident reporting, and model updates be assigned. The reasoning is that an unowned control may go unexecuted, so errors reach patients undetected. No study has measured whether named ownership raises the rate at which safety controls are actually carried out.

One commentary proposes that clear decision rights may reduce duplicated effort and help separate model failures from workflow or governance bottlenecks. This claim is untested. Health systems adopting the practice should expect staff time to build and maintain the role map, and they have no published cost or staffing estimate to plan against.

The NIST generative AI profile adds whistleblower protections for staff who report harm, and HEAAL asks that parties responsible for managing a tool across its lifecycle be identified. A documented role map could tell patients and staff whom to contact about a problem, though no study has examined whether it does.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems or AI deployments with and without documented governance role maps. Useful designs would measure whether controls such as monitoring, audits, and incident response are completed on schedule, how quickly problems are escalated and resolved, and how much staff time the mapping requires.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems with thin governance staffing may face greater difficulty assigning an owner to every control, and whether the practice works in those settings is unknown.
